10040-aleutian-indian-and-english-dictio:
Charles A. Lee compiled this Alaska Indian dictionary in 1896, giving common words in the dialects of the Aleutian Indian language. It covers the speech of the Oogashik, Egashik, Egegik, Anangashuk, and Misremie tribes around the Sulima River and neighboring parts.

The book pairs Aleutian words with English, offering a practical word list for traders, missionaries, and travelers in Alaska. Its value today is documentary: a record of languages and dialects as spoken in the nineteenth century. Linguists and historians of Alaska will find it a rare, useful survival for study today.
10341-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Charles F. Horne edited this twenty-first volume of The Great Events by Famous Historians, a series that retells world history in the words of leading scholars. Each volume arranges events in date order, with short introductions, notes, and reading lists to link the pieces. The plan claims no party, sect, or section bias.

This volume covers recent events around 1910 and 1911, from a house of governors in the United States to the union of South Africa and Portugal's turn to a republic. Finland under pressure, fast miles, and the fall of Diaz in Mexico also appear. Readers get a readable, early twentieth-century survey of a world on the move.
14017-clara-a-swain-m-d:
Mrs. Robert Hoskins told the life of Clara Swain in 1912, honoring the first woman doctor sent as a medical missionary to the women of India. Born in Elmira, New York, and raised in Castile, Swain was the youngest of ten children and a frail child. Sermons in Philadelphia stirred her faith, and she trained at the Woman's Medical College before sailing east.

India tested her skill and her patience. Secluded in zenanas, high-born women could see no male doctor, so Swain's presence opened doors no other medicine could enter. A ruler's support led to a women's dispensary opened in June 1885, with rooms in the palace itself. Hoskins writes with open admiration, yet the facts stand clear: one doctor, working among women shut from public care, built a lasting place for women's medicine in her district.
14500-two-dyaloges-c-1549-wrytten-in-lat:
This volume reprints two dialogues by Erasmus of Rotterdam, first written in Latin and translated into English by Edmonde Becke, printed at Canterbury in 1549. The transcriber kept the original spelling and punctuation.

One dialogue, Polyphemus or the Gospeller, mocks a man who parrots gospel phrases without living them, while the other disputes things and names. Cannius questions Polyphemus on prayer, fasting, and true piety, exposing hollow show. The dialogues show Erasmus's satiric humanism at work, and the Tudor English gives the text a special flavor for early modern readers. Becke's translation brought Erasmus to readers without Latin.
17057-the-submarine-boys-and-the-spies-d:
Victor G. Durham's fourth Submarine Boys book, from 1910, opens on Guess Day at Spruce Beach, where friends fret over a boat gone to the bottom once too often. Spies soon close in: Kamanako appears, a small Russian has his way, and Jack's crew falls into enemy power. A French rat in the corner, a secret service joke, and a gallant farewell to a foe follow.

The tale mixes undersea daring with spy games, as the boys dodge sharks of the deep in both senses. Durham keeps the action fast and the talk boyish, with honor held high even toward foes. Young fans of the series will find this one of its liveliest, with danger on shore and under water alike.
17058-the-submarine-boys-lightning-cruis:
Victor G. Durham wrote this 1910 fifth book of eight in the Submarine Boys series, The Young Kings of the Deep. Chapters move from a danger sign up and torpedo practice at last into a submerged foe and a submariner's revenge. A mysterious order, Judas and company, and Eph playing gallant follow. A full bag, fair sport, and red-hot metal appear. A trick seen through and a goal for the lightning cruise lead to Jack giving the order to fire. A message of terror, findings on the Thor, and a cornered captain close the tale.

Durham keeps Jack Benson and his crew at full speed, with torpedoes, foes, and narrow escapes under the sea. The tale is pure boys' adventure, with honor and nerve as its compass. Young readers get a fast, exciting cruise, full of dives, fights, and a crew that earns its royal nickname.
19416-illustrated-catalogue-of-a-portion:
William H. Holmes prepared this illustrated catalogue for the Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology, covering its field season of eighteen eighty-one. It lists objects gathered in North Carolina and Tennessee, chiefly from Cherokee country and from mounds along the Pigeon River. Stone tools, clay pots, and items of plant and animal matter each get their own entries.

One mound alone held dozens of burials, with large, well-kept shards of pottery found nearby. The catalogue is a plain record of what was dug up, where, and in what state, and it remains a base source for the early study of Native peoples of the southeast.
20801-some-remains-hitherto-unpublished-:
A changed word, from advice to direction, shows how Joseph Butler polished his thought. Some Remains gathers papers Butler never published in his life. Notes at the close of fragments show fresh ink where he reworked a line.

Butler, Bishop of Durham, wrote the famed Analogy of Religion in the 1700s. His sermons on human nature still shape moral thought today. These scraps let readers watch a careful mind at work in private. Scholars prize such remains for the light they throw on how a great thinker's views took their final shape.
2363-incognita-or-love-and-duty-reconcil:
William Congreve's early novel Incognita, or Love and Duty Reconcil'd, is a Restoration comedy in prose, full of disguises, mistaken lovers, and witty intrigue. Written when Congreve was still young, it follows Aurelian and Hippolito through a maze of love affairs in Florence, where duty and desire keep crossing. The prose sparkles with the wit that would fill his plays.

The novella is short, fast, and deliberately artificial, a game of masks and revelations. It shows Congreve learning the comic timing of The Way of the World. Readers of Restoration literature will enjoy this rare prose piece.
24046-john-eliot-s-first-indian-teacher-:
William Wallace Tooker published John Eliot's First Indian Teacher and Interpreter, Cockenoe-de-Long Island, in London in 1896, in a limited edition of 215 copies, this number 169. Tooker, a member of the Long Island Historical Society, tells the story of Cockenoe's career from the early records.

Eliot himself wrote, in a letter of December 2, 1648, that Cockenoe was the first he made use of to teach him words and to be his interpreter. From exceptional knowledge of English, traits of character, and strong personality, Cockenoe became a valued helper to the first English settlers. Connecticut and Massachusetts, the Commissioners of the United Colonies of New England, and the governor of New York all found occasion for his services in dealings with the Indians.
24403-the-young-lord-and-other-tales-to-:
Mrs. Crosland, late Camilla Toulmin, wrote these tales, published by Darton and Company in London in 1849 and 1850, with Victorine Durocher by Mrs. Sherwood. The Young Lord, and the Trial of Adversity, carries a text from Saint Matthew on treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust corrupts and thieves do not break through and steal. The opening tale asks how to reward a little boy who returned a bracelet lost at church.

Mrs. Sidney puts the question to her only son Charles, home for Midsummer with his widowed mother at a Devonshire cottage, his early home. Charles answers that people should not be rewarded for common honesty, since the clasp held his father's likeness, known to all the village. His mother replies that school has not weakened his selfish feelings, and that he wrests phrases from their meaning to serve himself. Readers get moral tales for the young.
26123-an-essay-on-slavery-and-abolitioni:
Catharine Beecher's 1837 essay answers a friend who asked why he should not join an abolition society. It grew from a private letter to Angelina Grimke, who planned to urge northern women into such societies. Beecher argues instead for mild, peaceful, and patient measures against slavery, holding up Wilberforce and like-minded reformers as models of forbearance.

The essay speaks straight to American women, urging them to use moral influence at home and in their communities rather than join campaigning societies. It remains a key text for the split inside the antislavery cause. On one side stood those who sought instant action. On the other stood those who feared haste would harden the South and wreck the Union.
27154-fibble-d-d:
Irvin S. Cobb's Fibble, D.D., published by Doran in 1916 with illustrations by Tony Sarg, collects episodes in the life of a certain young curate, subdivided into three parts. Cobb, known for Back Home and Paths of Glory, turns his humor on parish life.

One episode finds the narrator carried into a farm dwelling, confronted by a gaunt woman who trusts his abductors' rambling version, and given drugged milk of peculiar odour. The draught, oddly, restores his faculties at once, in a comic tangle worthy of the young curate's luck.
32089-memoir-of-jared-sparks-ll-d:
Brantz Mayer, president of the Maryland Historical Society, prepared this memoir of Jared Sparks at the society's request. Mayer read it before the society's annual meeting on February 7, 1867, and it was printed at Baltimore the same year. Sparks had been one of the society's earliest and most distinguished honorary members. Mayer calls the duty sad, but not entirely unpleasant, as he recalls a colleague and a public figure.

The memoir follows Sparks from youth to standing: through the help of President Kirkland, he entered Harvard University at twenty-two on a Pennoyer scholarship. Mayer judges him a biographer rather than a historian in the strict sense. He chose stirring epochs and prominent men who stood at the centre of great events at decisive moments. Readers get a short, respectful life of an American scholar of the early republic.
32530-armageddon-2419-a-d:
Philip Francis Nowlan's Armageddon--2419 A.D. drops a man from an earlier century among people of the twenty-fifth century. His first glimpse of a human being there is a boy in tight green garments and a helmet-like cap. He moves through woodland with a silent pistol that sets off explosions deep among the trees.

The boy leaps fifty feet through the air and lands with a strange, slowed grace, wearing a broad belt that bulks like a knapsack across his shoulders. Nowlan builds suspense from that first meeting, letting strange clothes, weapons, and movement hint at a changed world before the wider war of the future comes into view.
32624-a-history-of-rome-to-565-a-d:
Arthur E. R. Boak's A History of Rome to 565 A.D., published in New York in 1921, carries Roman history from Italy's forerunners to the empire's later centuries. Part one treats the geography of Italy, prehistoric civilization, and the peoples of historic Italy, including Etruscans and Greeks.

Later parts follow the early monarchy and republic, expansion to the unification of the peninsula, struggle with Carthage, Rome and the Greek east, and territorial growth across three continents. Boak, professor of ancient history at the University of Michigan, writes a textbook history grounded in sources for early Rome.
33155-medicina-flagellata-or-the-doctor-:
Medicina Flagellata, or The Doctor Scarify'd, printed in London in 1721, is a satire. It lays open the vices of the faculty of physicians and the insignificance of a great part of their materia medica. It also gives rules to discern the true physician from the empiric and useful medicine from noxious and trading physic. With an essay on health, it adds errors found in late writings on the plague, with rules for that distemper.

The book's Latin tags set its tone: medicine grows worse by doctoring, and if physicians fail you, let a cheerful mind, rest, and moderate diet be your physicians. Written when bleeding, purging, and patent remedies filled the shops, it speaks for patients against a powerful profession. As a document of early eighteenth-century medicine and satire, it remains sharp, funny, and surprisingly modern in its call for regimen over drugs.
35719-the-history-of-the-five-indian-nat:
The History of the Five Indian Nations was printed in 1747. Osborne sold Colden's history in London that year. Colden was surveyor-general of New York. A map of the Five Nations' country fronts the book. Its note counts the Tuscaroras a sixth nation already. A seventh was received at Albany in 1723, it adds. The title page promises a full account. Religion, manners, customs, laws, and government are treated. Battles and treaties with the European nations are set down. Wars with other Indians get their own relations. The present state of the trade is described last. The whole shows the gain of their alliance to Britain, Colden argues.

French intrigues to draw them away are exposed beside it. A dedication goes to General Oglethorpe. Indian affairs, Colden tells him, have always weighed with his judgement.
3617-widger-s-quotations-from-the-projec:
David Widger gathered this file of quotations from Alexandre Dumas's Celebrated Crimes, the ninth in his series of quotation books for Project Gutenberg. Dumas, famous for The Three Musketeers, also wrote a series of true crime histories about murder, poison, and intrigue in European courts. This file lifts short passages from those crime stories for browsing.

Readers meet Dumas's dramatic voice in brief form: tales of poisoners, queens, and assassins told with novelist's flair. The set works as a sampler for those curious about his nonfiction and as a source of short lines. His full Celebrated Crimes give the trials, escapes, and executions that these extracts only hint at.
36587-a-true-relation-of-the-apparition-:
Daniel Defoe's pamphlet A True Relation of the Apparition of One Mrs Veal was first published in 1706, and the text here comes from his collected Novels and Miscellaneous Works. The title page promises the apparition of Mrs Veal, the next day after her death, to Mrs Bargrave at Canterbury on the 8th of September, 1705.

A preface vouches for the tale through a chain of witnesses. A justice of the peace at Maidstone in Kent sent it to his friend in London, on the word of a kinswoman living near Mrs Bargrave. The apparition itself recommends the perusal of Drelincourt's Book of Consolations against the Fears of Death.
37083-through-shot-and-flame-the-adventu:
Through Shot and Flame is a war memoir by J D Kestell, issued by Methuen in 1903. Kestell served as chaplain to President Steyn and to General Christian de Wet in the field. He dedicates the book to his wife, one of thousands who endured in the struggle. With her he honours their son Charles, who died a prisoner at Ladysmith.

Part one, called Hope, opens as Kestell joins the Harrismith commando of the Boers. The adventures and experiences promised in the subtitle are a chaplain view of war. Faith, suffering, and loyalty under fire give the memoir its grave tone. South African war readers gain the Boer side told by a man of peace.
37683-chambers-s-twentieth-century-dicti:
Thomas Davidson edits a word book in Chambers's Twentieth Century Dictionary of the English Language, part 1 of 4, covering A to D. Chambers prints it in London and Edinburgh in 1908. The title page promises much: a book that pronounces and explains words, gives their roots, and adds phrases, trade terms, and full appendices, with many plates.

Davidson had aided on Chambers's Encyclopaedia and edited Chambers's English Dictionary. This is the third English dictionary which the present editor has prepared, his preface says. He may therefore lay claim to a long schooling in his trade. It is based upon his Library Dictionary of 1898, he notes, but will be found to have many useful traits of its own.
39612-the-life-of-a-conspirator-being-a-:
A descendant wrote this biography of Sir Everard Digby, the Gunpowder Plot conspirator, published in London in 1895. The contents begin with his portrait, his father's book, his days at the court of Queen Elizabeth, and his marriage and knighthood.

Later chapters follow his turn toward Rome: hospitality at Gothurst, Father Gerard, the question of underhandedness, and his conversion. Then comes the politics of the succession, the Bye Plot, and Guy Fawkes. The author, who also wrote a life of Archbishop Laud, treats persecution under Elizabeth and James as the ground of the story. Readers get a sympathetic family view of a famous plotter.
40225-america-discovered-by-the-welsh-in:
Bowen wrote this argument, America Discovered by the Welsh in 1170, printed at Philadelphia in 1876. A Welsh motto heads the title page, rendered beneath as the truth against the world. A preface opens with a bookseller's joke that turns into the book's first piece of evidence.

A clergyman from Rhode Island, Bowen tells us, brought a supposed Indian Bible to a New York antiquarian, who had promised five hundred dollars for one. Opened in the shop, the book proved to be a Welsh Bible, and the clergyman vanished with it. The two tongues, Bowen argues, are close kin in their letters and sounds. His pages then set out to fix belief in the voyages of Prince Madoc and his followers in 1170, and to give them their rightful place in the history of America.
40335-the-bath-keepers-or-paris-in-those:
The Bath Keepers, or Paris in Those Days, volume one, forms volume seven of the novels of Paul de Kock. George Barrie's Sons printed it in Boston and New York in 1903. A front plate shows Leodgard returning to his friends, pale and shifty eyed. The tale opens at two in the morning in 1634. Snow melts as it falls on the Rue Couture-Sainte-Catherine. Paris lies black and unlit, with no lanterns, gas, or lamps.

The narrator jokes that a man who invented such light then might face torture for magic. Few folk walked the streets late, and the watch was weak. Young nobles beat the watch as a sport, with little fear. Richelieu's single theatre stands against a bare stage scene. The novel promises period colour and intrigue.
40518-the-bath-keepers-or-paris-in-those:
Paul de Kock continues a Paris tale in the second volume of The Bath Keepers, printed at Boston in an edition of his novels. Chapter twenty-nine opens on a stormy night at the bath house on Rue Saint-Jacques. Ambroisine waits alone for her father while thunder and rain beat outside.

Master Hugonnet comes home drunk, leaning on a wine shop keeper who saw him beat a small solicitor's clerk half to death. Once home, the bath keeper weeps over the deed and calls it a shame, not knowing the victim was beaten by his own hand. Ambroisine, used to reading his drunkenness by the weight of his knock, sets him straight. Readers get de Kock's mix of farce, sentiment, and Paris street life in full swing.
42538-the-round-towers-of-ireland-or-the:
Henry O’Brien wrote The Round Towers of Ireland, a bold claim on the towers’ first builders. W Thacker and Company issued this new edition in London in eighteen hundred ninety eight. Seven hundred fifty copies were printed, then the type was spread. This copy stands as number three hundred twenty four of that run.

O’Brien ties the towers to the Tuath-De-Danaans of old myth. A long front tale tells how the Royal Irish Academy spurned him. A prize for the best tower essay went to Petrie instead. A £100 gift from Lord Cloncurry went with that same award. O’Brien first wrote thanks in sharp irony to the group. Plain rage at named men then burst through his mask. His text runs past five hundred pages of proof and lore. A list of chief Irish towers and crosses ends the book.
43094-thy-sea-is-great-our-boats-are-sma:
Henry Van Dyke wrote Thy Sea is Great, Our Boats are Small in 1922. Fleming H Revell Company issued the hymn book. Seven new hymns fill its main part. Three earlier hymns join at the back. Voyagers opens the set at page nine. Its text comes from Psalm ninety-five.

The sea is his, and he made it, that text says. O Maker of the mighty deep, the hymn sings. Keep watch above our life's adventure, it prays. Thy sea is great, our boats are small, it ends. Secret tides may help or delay us, it admits. Tempests lurk and fogs hang grey, it adds. Homeward bound, we ask for harbor lights of friendship. A hymn of labor and a hymn of joy follow. A peace hymn of the republic closes it. Van Dyke's hymns gave churches a seafarer's trust in God.
43856-the-boy-chums-cruising-in-florida-:
Wilmer Ely wrote this boys' tale of the Florida fishing fleet, printed at New York in 1914. The Boy Chums had met readers in tales of Indian River, the Gulf of Mexico, and Haunted Island. Here four friends ship out into Florida waters for work and sport.

The chums call on Daniels, a busy man of the fleet, and settle in for the cruise. Chapters bring a night alarm, a warning, a strange light at midnight, and a ghost. Grouper banks, a storm, castaways, and smugglers crowd the later pages. A find of treasure trove caps the fun. The tale mixes sea work, good friends, and steady peril.
45079-the-art-of-graining-how-acquired-a:
The Art of Graining: How Acquired and How Produced, by Charles Pickert and A Metcalf, teaches painters to imitate wood for interior finishing, with descriptions of colours and their applications. D Van Nostrand published the manual at New York in 1872, with 42 coloured plates on stone showing the various woods.

The introduction argues that trained skill alone perfects the imitation, and urges learners to practise drawing the sample copies with narrow and broad-pointed pencils. The authors offer the fruit of long experience as a reliable guide for brother artisans. Oak and black walnut get the fullest treatment as the chief woods to copy.
51376-historical-record-of-the-fourth-or:
Richard Cannon compiles the Historical Record of the Fourth, or Royal Irish Regiment of Dragoon Guards for the official Historical Records of the British Army. The series was prepared under the Adjutant-General's direction by command of William the Fourth, and printed at London by William Clowes and Sons. General orders from Horse-Guards, dated January 1, 1836, head the volume.

Those orders, signed by Lord Hill and Adjutant-General John Macdonald, require each regiment's account to give its formation, stations, battles and captured trophies. Names of officers and men killed, wounded or specially distinguished, and the causes of badges and devices, must also be recorded.
51907-verses-of-a-v-a-d:
Verses of a V-A-D is a book of war poems by Vera Brittain, first published in August 1918. Brittain served as a Voluntary Aid Detachment nurse, and her service mark stands on the title page. The book is dedicated to the memory of Roland Aubrey Leighton, a lieutenant in the Worcestershire Regiment. He died of wounds near Hébuterne on December 23, 1915, and his own farewell verse is printed with the dedication.

The contents begin with August 1914 and a poem at St Pancras Station in August 1915. A military hospital, the sisters buried at Lemnos, and the German ward follow. Other poems address a fallen idol, the only son, and her brother. The volume is a young nurse's record of love, nursing, and loss in the Great War.
53281-the-child-of-the-moat-a-story-for-:
Ian Stoughton Holborn wrote a story for girls set in the year 1557, published at New York in 1916. A plan of the hall at Holwick in Yorkshire, with its buttery, pantry, and chapel marked, orients the reader. The contents open with a chapter simply called Hate.

Prisoners, thieves, bitterness, and remorse follow in the early chapters, then a packman's visit and swords and questionings. A desperate task, a ride to Carlisle, and a diplomatic victory lead to persecution and torture. The battle of Liddisdale, a birthday party, and the great iron chest close the tale. A poem from the author's Children of Fancy heads the first chapter, casting children as exorcists of despair.
55074-the-cruise-of-the-sally-d:
James Otis wrote this boys cruise tale of the schooner Sally D. Grosset and Dunlap printed it in New York for young readers. Contents open with Uncle Ben advice, then the rescue at sea. War declared and a matter of business fill early chapters.

An unwelcome visitor, a pitched battle, and Uncle Ben arrival follow. A stranded schooner, a proposition, and the schooner for sale come. Shipowners, wrecking, and the baby fill the middle of the tale. Uncle Ben whittles driftwood as the boy waits for his word. The launching, trial trip, first cruise, and getting even fill the later chapter heads.
55536-historical-record-of-the-sixth-or-:
Richard Cannon's record of the Sixth, or Inniskilling, Regiment of Dragoons, printed in London in 1847, gives the regiment's formation in 1689 and its services down to 1846. Plates show the guidons, and the uniform as worn in 1742, 1825, and 1843. The book was compiled at the Adjutant General's Office at Horse Guards.

It opens with the General Orders of 1 January 1836, by which the King commanded that an account of every regiment in the British Army be published. Each account was to give the formation and stations, the battles and sieges, and the names of officers and men killed or wounded. Gallant conduct, badges, and devices were to be recorded as well.
55555-the-golden-rule-cook-book-six-hund:
The Golden Rule Cook Book, gathered and arranged by MRL Sharpe, holds six hundred recipes for dishes without meat. A new edition was published in Boston in 1912.

The opening pages argue the case for a meatless table, citing disease found in sold meat and quoting the book of Genesis on plants given for food. Sections then cover the kitchen, the dining room, and general advice. Recipes run through soups, vegetables, nut dishes, rice and macaroni, croquettes, sauces, eggs, cheese, and salads. Later pages give savouries, sandwiches, pastry, hot breads, plum pudding, and mince pie without meat. A chapter of menus and an index close the book.
55959-the-coming-of-the-white-men-storie:
The Coming of the White Men tells stories of how our country was discovered. Mary Hazelton Wade wrote the book for young American readers. Wilde of Boston and Chicago held the rights in the year 1905. Sears Gallagher drew the illustrations, the Norsemen among the plates. Wade had writ Ten Little Indians and the Little Cousin series.

Fourteen chapters run from the Norsemen to the poor debtors of Georgia. The Genoese sailor, John Cabot and the codfish, follow in order. The fountain of youth and the good knight fill the next tales. Henry Hudson, the Pilgrims, and little pilgrims of long ago come next. Roger Williams and the father of waters carry the story westward. Lord Baltimore and the Catholics close the discovery tales here. Uncle Sam, tall and thin with a tuft of chin hair, tells them. Joe and Lucy listen at their cosy village storyteller's knee.
56082-dream-songs-for-the-belove-d:
Dream Songs for the Beloved, by Eleanor Farjeon, was printed in London in spring 1911 as number five in the Orpheus Series. Farjeon had also written Pan Worship. The first poem in the book is a song to her mother.

Farjeon says songs she cannot sing fly round her thoughts like birds. Her mother song has the highest wing of all, past her power to follow. The list holds In Love House, Double Beauty, and a piece set in 440 BC, the year before Christ. Other songs name fog, poplars at night, wild hyacinth, and silence. A longer piece treats Weland and the swan girls from old lore. Readers get soft, musical verse of love and dream.
56380-doctor-mead-s-short-discourse-expl:
Doctor Mead's Short Discourse Explain'd is an anonymous pamphlet printed at London in 1721. It promises a clearer account of pestilential contagion and preventing, in answer to the celebrated Doctor Mead's short discourse on the plague. The writer opens by noting the many and various opinions about the design and meaning of Mead's book.

The greatest number of people of all ranks, the pamphlet says, expected easy rules from the book, whereby they might govern their life against so silent an enemy as the pestilence. The great demand for it ceased of a sudden. Folk found the physician had no hand in it, or that his rules were locked up for the favourites of his faculty. The writer holds that the people commonly make the best judgment of things after a little experience. The pamphlet speaks for lay readers who wanted plain plague counsel.
57172-life-and-adventures-of-frances-nam:
Frances Namon Sorcho is presented in this little book as the only woman deep sea diver in the world, working with Captain Louis Sorcho's Great Deep Sea Diving Company. A long poem at the front, The Bottom of the Sea, sings of the wondrous wealth unknown at the bottom of the sea. There stately ships rot on Neptune's throne and jewels flash in caverns.

The poem's last figure is the diver herself, an humble hero of the deep. In armor, helmet, and shoes of lead, she creeps in sunken hulls among the million dead to wrest the golden treasure heap. The preface then states the book's object plainly: to enlighten patrons on how divers exist in the depths. It promises the strange costume they must wear, the sensations they feel, and the sights they see. The desperate risks they take had been a sealed volume to the public before.
59723-history-of-the-jesuits-their-origi:
Nicolini's History of the Jesuits, their origin, progress, doctrines and designs, was published in London by Bohn in 1854. Nicolini, of Rome, had already written a history of the pontificate of Pius the Ninth and a life of Father Gavazzi. A portrait of Loyola, after Rubens, forms the frontispiece.

The preface states the author's aim plainly. Nicolini set out to give readers a just and correct idea of the character and aims of the brotherhood of Loyola. He calls the Jesuits the greatest enemies of liberal institutions and of civil and religious freedom. He also claims that no serious and complete history of the Society existed before his own. The book argues that England, above all, should watch the order's present activity.
62865-gibson-new-cartoons-a-book-of-char:
Gibson New Cartoons is a book of drawings by Charles Dana Gibson. Scribner's Sons published it in New York in 1916. Its subtitle calls it a book of Gibson's latest drawings. Many had first appeared in Life magazine between 1912 and 1916. Thanks are given to Life for leave to reprint them. The pages pair each drawing with a short caption dialogue. A girl in Tipperary points to her heart in one. Another jokes about three hundred dollars for a gown.

Other captions trade lines between husbands and wives at home. A little sister asks what a widow is in one exchange. Her big sister answers that a widow is a lady who has had a husband. She adds that the lady is going to have another. Courtship, marriage, and money are the standing themes. The Gibson Girl's creator works here in light social comedy.
64604-the-gibson-book-a-collection-of-pu:
The Gibson Book, a collection of the published works of Charles Dana Gibson in two volumes, appeared at New York in 1906 from Charles Scribner's Sons. Volume two is held here. Eleven Gibson books are gathered into the two volumes, by arrangement with Harper and Brothers, publishers of seven of them.

The drawings speak through their captions. One long sequence follows a widow and her friends. She contemplates the cloister, and decides to die in spite of her doctor. Exercise is no cure for her spirits. She endures a call from Miss Babbles, the authoress, who reads aloud. She takes a quiet dinner with the doctor, receives a message from the outside world, and draws hostile criticism for her retirement. Gibson's pen records the manners of his day in these captioned scenes.
64843-around-the-black-sea-asia-minor-ar:
William Eleroy Curtis toured the lands round the Black Sea and wrote them up as newspaper letters. Around the Black Sea gathers those letters into a book. It came out in 1911.

The letters were written in the summer and autumn of 1910. They ran in the Chicago Record-Herald, whose late editor the book honours. The route takes in Asia Minor, Armenia and the Caucasus. Circassia, Daghestan, the Crimea and Roumania round out the ring. A full map of the sea and its shores sits inside the back cover. Curtis writes as a brisk, keen eyed reporter. Curtis had roamed Turkestan and Syria for the same press.
65245-emblems-of-mortality-representing-:
Emblems of Mortality is a picture book of death, printed in London for Hodgson in 1789. More than fifty cuts show Death seizing people of all ranks and degrees. The cuts copy a famous painting in the churchyard of the Dominican church at Basel in Switzerland.

Each cut has a short address in verse, turned from the Latin and French. A long preface tells the history of this dance of death and of like paintings in Europe. It traces the Basel work to the great council that sat there from 1431. Plague struck the city in 1439, while popes and princes were present. The book was meant for the curious, and for the teaching and delight of youth.
6721-the-voyages-of-captain-scott-retold:
Charles Turley retells Captain Robert Scott's voyages from The Voyage of the Discovery and Scott's Last Expedition, with an introduction by J. M. Barrie. Pictures in color and black and white, plus a map, aid the tale. The Discovery chapters run from southward ho to winter quarters, a polar winter, and a southern journey, then a second winter and release.

The last expedition chapters follow stormy seas, depôt laying at One Ton Camp, and perils that end in tragedy. Turley writes for young readers, with a hero's tale told plainly. The Voyages of Captain Scott is a moving, classic retelling of Antarctic courage and loss.
67504-a-woman-s-quest-the-life-of-marie-:
Agnes Vietor, a surgeon who taught at the Woman's Medical College in New York, edited the life of Marie Zakrzewska, printed in 1924. Zakrzewska lived from 1829 to 1902. A photograph from the sixties stands at the front. She rose to head of midwives at the Royal Hospital Charité in Berlin.

Later she crossed to America. She served as first house doctor at the New York Infirmary for Women and Children. In Boston she founded a hospital for women and children and led its work. Contents trace her Berlin childhood, school, and first sight of hospitals. Her mother's midwife work drew her in, and a diploma made her a teacher of the art.
69143-the-book-of-artemas-concerning-men:
Doran of New York issued a war tale in the voice of the old Bible, with rights held from 1917 and 1918. Artemas, a scribe in Lon in the land of En, keeps the tale. His book is given to Eve on the gift page.

Peace lay on the land of Eur, but Willi, who ruled the men of Hu, was sly and grasping. His son Mud, proud and empty, urged him on with sweet words on his might. A tale of an oak tree and its sense starts the path to war. Names are veiled, but the kings, lands, and greed of the great war show through the old style at once.
6989-ancient-rome-from-the-earliest-time:
Robert Pennell wrote Ancient Rome as a companion to his History of Greece, for high schools and academies wanting a short clear account of Rome's rise and fall. The revised edition was wholly rewritten, with new matter added to meet recent requirements and the penults of proper names marked long in text and index. Lives of chief men join an outline of institutions, manners, and religion.

Examination papers show the present range of requirement in leading colleges, and maps and plans were specially drawn and engraved for the book. Names and places not in the text were mostly left off the maps, to keep them clear and open. Pennell aims at a school history that is brief, orderly, and easy to use.
69922-dairying-exemplified-or-the-busine:
Twamley's treatise on cheese-making, in a second edition corrected and improved, was printed at Warwick for the author in 1787 and sold in London at two shillings. Its rules were collected from the most experienced dairy-women of several counties. They rest on thirty years of the author's own practice in the cheese trade.

Twamley addresses his preface to the dairy-women of Great Britain, from whom his first hints came. His design is to help those not fully acquainted with the right management of a dairy, and to better the quality and enlarge the quantity of cheese through the kingdom. The second edition drops his treatises on orchards and vegetation to keep the price moderate.
70210-a-select-glossary-of-english-words:
Richard Chenevix Trench, the archbishop and student of words, wrote this select glossary of English words used formerly in senses different from their present ones. Kegan Paul, Trench and Company published this seventh edition of 1890, revised by Mayhew. His motto runs: things flee away, words remain.

Trench's preface says the book traces, in a popular manner for general readers, the changes of meaning that familiar words have undergone on English lips. He argues that as fewer students enjoy Latin and Greek, the study of their own language offers the best substitute discipline for the mind. Taking a classic apart word by word, he suggests, shows how many words once meant something quite other than they mean now. The glossary gives entry after entry of such changed words.
71262-the-magazine-of-history-with-notes:
The Magazine of History with Notes and Queries, volume II, number 6, appeared at New York in December 1905. William Abbatt published it monthly at 281 Fourth Avenue, at $5.00 a year and 50 cents a number. The contents are largely Revolutionary War material.

Griffis contributes a second paper on Sullivan's great march into the Indian country. Schuyler concludes an essay on the liberty of the press, and Hendrick writes on Bushnell's Turtle. Other pieces treat relics of Commodore John Barry in Philadelphia and Captain James Duncan's diary of the siege of Yorktown. Original documents print letters of Washington and of Joseph Trumbull. Minor topics, Indiana county names and book notices close the number.
72497-date-of-publication-2083-a-d:
William Morrison wrote Date of Publication 2083, a science tale printed in Fantastic Universe in the autumn of nineteen fifty-three. A head note jokes that lending libraries have made mistakes, but never one so loaded as sending Carrie the wrong volume. Carrie Samason had reserved The Perfect Hostess months before. A postcard says the book is held for her, to be called for in two days.

Carrie sends her son James, age eleven, to fetch the book on pain of losing his allowance. James stops to pitch a baseball game on the way home, and the book sits forgotten in the parlor. The tale's frame tells of hypnotism, an art older than man, made science in the days of Mesmer. What the library sent home by mistake drives the plot.
77795-the-voyage-of-the-norman-d:
Barbara Newhall Follett wrote The Voyage of the Norman D in 1928. Alfred A Knopf issued it at New York and London. Follett had written The House Without Windows in 1927. A cabin boy tells this sea tale, the title says. The book grew from a long letter to a friend. She mailed it in eight-page typed parts.

A publisher's note lays out the book's making. Purely private passages were cut for print. Much haste-born repeat matter was weeded out. The schooner's true name stands disguised here. Some crew names hide as well. Her day notes ran just four pages in all. Weather and progress filled those brief lines. A young sailor's full, clear memory does the rest. Sea writing of rare freshness, the book tells a working voyage as a girl lived and loved it.
7808-grand-daddy-whiskers-m-d:
Nellie M. Leonard's Grand-Daddy Whiskers, M.D., pictured by Carle Michel Boog, sends a woodland doctor to work among animal folk. A message from the woodfolk leads back to the lake, where Grand-Daddy begins his rounds, Dot Squeaky holds summer school, and a woods fire tests them all.

Later chapters bring a busy day, twin tails, Wiggle borrowing an automobile, autumn leaves, and being snowed in. Pictures show blindfold games, a call to Pond Lily Lake, a broken limb set deftly, and a band playing Silvy's Waltz. It is a cozy animal tale of care, courage, and neighbors helping.
79468-our-mission-to-the-court-of-marocc:
Our Mission to the Court of Marocco in 1880, under Sir John Drummond Hay, by Philip Durham Trotter, was published by David Douglas of Edinburgh in 1881. Trotter was a captain in the 93rd Highlanders. Sir John was Her Majesty's minister plenipotentiary and envoy extraordinary to the Sultan. Photographs by the Honourable D Lawless, of the Rifle Brigade, illustrate the book.

Trotter says plainly that the work is his diary, kept day by day during the mission and worked up for print. A fever caught in Morocco or at Gibraltar delayed the book and, he fears, hurt its style. The mission's events, he grants, are not startling. The value lies in a close look at the Sharifian court and the country: the road, the audiences, the gifts, and the etiquette of an empire then closed to most Europeans.
79520-the-benefit-of-farting-explain-d:
The Benefit of Farting Explained is a mock medical pamphlet, here in its thirteenth edition with additions. Its full title gives the game away in the style of a grave treatise. Most of the disorders of the fair sex, it claims, are owing to wind not duly vented in season. The work pretends to be written in Spanish by a professor of bombast at a nonsense university, and Englished for a lady of a matching nonsense shire.

Verses at the front state the doctrine in rhyme. A fart, though wholesome, does not fail, if barred of passage, to fly back to the head again. There its fumes disturb the brain. Gunpowder confined grows stronger the closer it is rammed, the poet adds. Fired in open air, it spends its force in harmless smoke. Physicians of a college, in jest, revised and approved the edition.
9803-memoirs-of-the-life-and-corresponde:
Volume two of John Knox Laughton's Memoirs of Henry Reeve covers Reeve's later life, from the Italian war to retirement. Chapters follow the war in Italy, literature and politics, law and letters, and church politics. The Franco-German war, the Greville memoirs, and Foxholes follow, with French royalists and a final change. Reeve, editor and man of letters, moves through Europe's great hours.

Laughton draws on Reeve's letters and diaries, with a portrait from a Rupert Potter photograph. The volume opens with Orsini's 1858 attempt on Napoleon III. A reader gets a rich Victorian life, told through letters, wars, and literary London.
9822-mrs-mary-robinson-written-by-hersel:
Mary Robinson, the actress and poet known as Perdita, wrote her own life story, and this edition adds lives of the Duchesses of Gordon and Devonshire. Robinson rose from a difficult youth to the London stage, where her beauty and talent made her one of the most talked-about women of her day.

Her memoir moves through theatre, fashion, love affairs, and debt with unusual frankness for its time. The added duchess biographies set her beside two other famous society women. Together they paint Georgian high society from inside, in the voices of women who lived at its center.
aleutian-indian-and-english-dictionary-c: Charles A. Lee compiles a dictionary of common words in the Aleut dialects spoken around the Sulima River and neighbouring parts of the Alaska Peninsula. Entries cover everyday things such as book, paper, and letter, together with numbers and money, in the speech of the Oogashik, Egashik, Anangashuk, and Misremie tribes. The little volume preserves a record of Alaskan Native language as heard in the field.
ancient-rome-from-the-earliest-times-dow:
Robert F. Pennell designed his history, by his preface, as a companion to his History of Greece. It fills a want in high schools and academies. They needed a short, clear statement of the rise and fall of Rome. It adds biography of her chief men. It outlines her institutions, manners, and religion. This revised edition was entirely rewritten, with maps and plans drawn for the book.

Fifty chapters run from the geography of Italy and the Tarquin dynasty to the plebeians' contest for rights and the Punic Wars. Caesar and Cicero, the empire, and the long decline to the year 476 follow. Examination papers at the back show the college standard of the day. Pennell's compact survey served classrooms for decades.
britannica-1911-abancourt-charles-xavier:
Charles Xavier Joseph de Franqueville d'Abancourt receives a short life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abancourt, nephew of Calonne, became Louis the Sixteenth's last minister of war in July 1792. He planned the defence of the Tuileries for the tenth of August.

Ordered by the Assembly to send the Swiss guards away, he refused, and was held for treason and sent to Orleans for trial. A transfer to Paris under Fournier, called the American, brought the party to Versailles. News of the Paris massacres met them there. Abancourt and his fellow prisoners were murdered in cold blood on the eighth of September. Fournier bore a charge of sharing the crime that the entry calls unjust.
britannica-1911-abano-pietro-d:
Pietro d'Abano receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Abano, also Petrus de Apono, was an Italian doctor and thinker born at Abano in 1250, or 1246 by some counts. Paris trained him in medicine and philosophy before Padua took him and his fame.

High fees and star lore fed a charge of magic against him: gold paid away flew back to his purse, men said, and he held the philosopher's stone. The Inquisition tried him twice; cleared once, he died in 1316 before the second trial closed. Guilt was still declared, and his effigy burned in place of a body friends had hidden. His Conciliator joins doctors and thinkers, and a book on poisons keeps his name.
britannica-1911-agoult-marie-catherine-s:
Marie Catherine Sophie de Flavigny, comtesse d'Agoult (1805-1876), was a French author. Daniel Stern was her pen name. She was born at Frankfort-on-Main in December 1805. Her father was a French emigrant officer. Her mother was a Frankfort banker's daughter. In 1827 she married the comte Charles d'Agoult. Her Paris salon gathered brilliant company. Vigny, Sainte-Beuve, Chopin, and Heine all frequented it.

Separation and Liszt reshaped her life. She became Franz Liszt's mistress for years. Three children came from that union. Cosima, her daughter, later married Richard Wagner. Her novel Nelida told the breach thinly disguised. Politics claimed her pen after 1848. Her salon turned revolutionary in tone then. Her History of the Revolution of 1848 ran three volumes.
britannica-1911-aguesseau-henri-francois:
Aguesseau, Henri Francois d', chancellor of France from 1668 to 1751, receives a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Limoges into a family of magistrates, he was raised by a father who held high posts across France. His upbringing carried a Jansenist tinge, a strict Catholic movement of the time, and he studied law under Jean Domat. At barely twenty-one he became an advocate-general to the parlement of Paris.

Legal reform made his name, covering gifts, wills, and successions, court procedure, and the limits of each court's power. His aim was uniform law across the provinces, work the entry calls an epoch in French law. Aguesseau served as chancellor three times, losing and regaining the seals amid court politics. His writings range from a treatise on money to theological essays, metaphysical meditations, and a life of his father that records his own early schooling.
britannica-1911-ailly-pierre-d:
Ailly, Pierre d', a French theologian of 1350 to 1420, receives a long entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Compiegne to a bourgeois family, he studied at Paris in the celebrated college of Navarre. He rose through its degrees quickly, taking his doctorate in theology in 1381. By then Western Christendom was split between two popes, Urban VI and Clement VII.

Ending that schism, the church's great division, became Ailly's cause. He backed the university of Paris when it called in 1381 for a general council to settle the matter, and argued the case before the king's council. Years of effort followed, including a plan to bring both popes to one coastal town for a double abdication. Discouraged by failure, he withdrew to his diocese of Cambrai in 1408, still loyal to Benedict XIII while French clergy moved against him.
britannica-1911-albuquerque-alphonso-d:
Albuquerque, Alphonso d', surnamed the Great and the Portuguese Mars, who lived from 1453 to 1515, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Lisbon, he was linked by descent to Portugal's royal family and educated at Alphonso V's court. After service in Africa he became chief equerry to John II. In 1503 he sailed on his first expedition to the East.

Rounding the Cape of Good Hope, Albuquerque secured the king of Cochin on his throne and won leave to build a Portuguese fort there. That fort laid the foundation of Portugal's eastern empire. King Emmanuel gave him a squadron command on his return. Later campaigns brought storms and shipwreck, including the loss of his treasure ship Flor de la Mar. At Goa he crushed a serious revolt under Idalcan and made the town the most flourishing Portuguese settlement in India.
britannica-1911-annunzio-gabriele-d:
Gabriele d'Annunzio, an Italian novelist and poet born at Pescara in eighteen sixty three, was of Dalmatian stock. His first years were spent free in the open fields. At sixteen he was sent to school in Tuscany. While still at school he brought out a small book of verse. It mixed bold copies of a poet then in vogue with Latin versions of real grace.

A critic praised the unknown youth and brought him before the public. The young poet then went to Rome and joined a noted group of writers there. Books of verse and prose followed in quick order in the early eighteen eighties. His prose tales dealt with peasant life in his home province of Abruzzi. New books of poems came in the years after.
britannica-1911-anville-jean-baptiste-bo:
Jean Baptiste Bourguignon d'Anville lived from 1697 to 1782. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls him perhaps the greatest map writer of his century. Born in Paris, he drew maps for Latin authors at twelve. His first real map, of ancient Greece, came out when he was fifteen. At twenty two he was named one of the king's map makers.

His aim was to purge maps of blind copying. Old maps had been traced from older ones for ages. He tested each place name against all the written proof he could find. Names with weak support were struck off the map. Whole lands shrank to blank space under that rule. He read widely to do it: tales of travel, poems, speeches, and more. Early work meant maps that lit up the books of travellers. His atlas for a history of China came out at the Hague in 1737.
britannica-1911-arbois-de-jubainville-ma:
Marie Henri d'Arbois de Jubainville (1827–1910) was a French historian and philologist. He was born at Nancy in December 1827. The École des Chartes trained him as archivist. He left it in 1851. The Aube departmental archives became his charge. He remained there until 1880. Retirement on a pension followed then. His Champagne history ran to eight volumes.

That work covered dukes and counts to the eleventh century. Inventorial abstracts filled several other volumes. An archaeological repertory appeared in 1861. Ancient Gaul's inhabitants attracted him next. His Premiers Habitants de l'Europe appeared in 1877. Celtic languages then consumed his efforts. He became an authority in that field. The Collège de France created a Celtic chair in 1882. He was its first appointee. He died in February 1910. His disciples honoured him with a memorial volume.
britannica-1911-aubigne-theodore-agrippa:
French poet and historian Theodore Agrippa d'Aubigne, born in Saintonge in fifteen fifty two, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His second name marks that his mother died in giving birth. As a child he showed a great gift for tongues.

By his own account he knew Latin, Greek, and Hebrew at age six. He had rendered a work of Plato before he was eleven. His father, a Huguenot tied to a failed plot, urged him to avenge the plotters' deaths. The boy had to flee Paris to escape harm. At fourteen he was at the siege of Orleans, where his father was killed. He later joined the Huguenot army.
britannica-1911-aubusson-pierre-d:
Pierre d'Aubusson (1423-1503) was grand master of the order of St John of Jerusalem and a keen foe of the Turks, as this 1911 Britannica article recounts. Born into a noble French family, he gave his early life to soldiering in the service of the emperor Sigismund. Under the archduke Albert of Austria he fought against the Turks.

Back in France, Aubusson sided with the Armagnacs against the Swiss and won great note at the battle of St Jacob in 1444. He then joined the knights of Rhodes, led an expedition against the pirates of the Levant, and rose to the highest offices in the order. In 1476 he was elected grand master. That was the age of the conquests of Mahommed II, who now began to threaten Europe, and in December 1479 a large Turkish fleet appeared.
britannica-1911-aumale-henri-eugene-phil:
Henri Eugene Philippe Louis d'Orleans, duc d'Aumale (1822-1897), was a French prince and statesman. He was the fifth son of Louis Philippe, duke of Orleans and later king of the French. He was born at Paris on 16 January 1822. While still young he gained a large fortune from the prince de Conde. He went to the college of Henri IV and left at seventeen to join the army as a captain.

Aumale marked himself out in the conquest of Algeria and was made governor of that colony. In that post he took the submission of the amir Abd-el-Kader. After the revolt of 1848 he withdrew to England. There he gave his time to the study of history and of war. In 1861 he fired back at Prince Napoleon's attacks on the house of Orleans. At the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War he offered his service.
britannica-1911-d:
D is a letter article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the fourth letter of the English alphabet. The Phoenician name Daleth answers to the Greek Delta. In form, the article says, D has changed little through its career. The earliest Phoenician shape was a triangle, and the rounded back that Latin passed to western Europe came from the Greeks of south west Italy.

The sound D stands for is the voiced dental that answers to the unvoiced t. The English d is in truth an alveolar, made with the tongue against the teeth sockets rather than the teeth. In true English words the letter mostly goes back to an Indo-European dh, in some words to a t.
britannica-1911-entrecasteaux-joseph-ant:
Entrecasteaux, Joseph-Antoine Bruni d' (1739–1793), was a French navigator born at Aix in 1739. He entered the navy at fifteen. In the war of 1778 he commanded a frigate of thirty-two guns and, by clever seamanship, convoyed a fleet of merchant ships from Marseilles to the Levant.

In 1785 Entrecasteaux took command of the French fleet in the East Indies, and two years later he was named governor of Mauritius and the Isle of Bourbon. In 1791 the French government chose him to lead an expedition seeking news of La Pérouse, unheard of since February 1788. His ships were the Recherche and the L'Esperance. No word of the missing navigator was found, but the search made real finds. He traced the east coast of New Caledonia and surveyed the Tasmanian coast, naming the d'Entrecasteaux Channel and Bruni Island. Near Java he was struck by scurvy and died on 20 July 1793.
britannica-1911-epinay-louise-florence-p:
Louise d'Epinay, a French writer, is the subject of a life story in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Valenciennes in seventeen twenty six, she lost her father in battle when she was nineteen. She wed her cousin, who was made a chief tax collector. That marriage proved unhappy, the entry says.

She gained a formal parting from her husband in seventeen forty nine. She then settled at a chateau in the valley of Montmorency. There she received many noted guests. The entry stresses her close ties to Rousseau and to Baron von Grimm. She also knew Diderot and other French men of letters of her age.
britannica-1911-epremesnil-jean-jacques-:
Jean Jacques Duval d Epremesnil, a French magistrate and politician who lived from 1745 to 1794, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in India at Pondicherry on 5 December 1745, he was the son of a colleague of Dupleix. He came back to France in 1750 and was educated in Paris for the law. In 1775 he became a counsellor in the parlement of Paris.

There Epremesnil soon stood out for his zealous defence of the rights of the parlement against the crown. He showed bitter enmity to Marie Antoinette in the affair of the diamond necklace. On 19 November 1787 he spoke for the parlement in demanding a call of the states general. When the court struck back with an edict that cut the functions of the parlement, he bribed printers to give him a copy before it was published.
britannica-1911-espinay-timoleon-d:
Timoleon d Espinay, who lived from 1580 to 1644, was a French soldier. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his chief posts in brief. He was the eldest of four sons of a noted lord. He held his father title as marquis de Saint Luc.

In 1603 Espinay went with Sully on an embassy to London. By 1622 he served as vice admiral of France. At sea he won ground against the defenders of La Rochelle. His pressure forced the Huguenot chief Soubise off two islands. Those isles, Re and Oleron, guarded the port approaches. In 1627 the crown made him lieutenant general of Guienne. The same year brought him the baton of a marshal of France.
britannica-1911-estaing-charles-hector-c:
Charles Hector, comte d'Estaing, a French admiral who lived from 1729 to 1794, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Ruvel in Auvergne, he entered the army as a colonel and sailed with Count de Lally to the East Indies in 1757. Taken at Madras in 1759, he was freed on parole, then held at Portsmouth on a charge of breaking it.

By 1777 he was vice admiral, and in 1778 he led a fleet to aid the United States. He blockaded Howe at Sandy Hook but did not strike, and a storm broke up his joint attack on Newport. In the West Indies he took St Vincent and Grenada, but his attack on Savannah was beaten off with heavy loss. Back in France he backed reform yet stood by the royal family, and his defence of Marie Antoinette led to his own death in 1794.
britannica-1911-estouteville-guillaume-d:
Guillaume d'Estouteville, a French churchman who lived from 1403 to 1483, gets a short career entry in the 1911 Britannica. His posts piled up across two lands. He was bishop of Angers, Digne, Porto, and Ostia, and archbishop of Rouen. He also held abbeys at Mont St Michel, St Ouen, and Montebourg.

Pope Nicholas the Fifth sent him to France as legate in 1451 to make peace between Charles the Seventh and England. In that role he took charge of the review of the trial of Joan of Arc. He also reformed the statutes of the university of Paris. He then led the clergy meeting at Bourges on the Pragmatic Sanction. Most of his last years passed at Rome. The entry calls him a great builder, with fine works at Rouen, Mont St Michel, Pontoise, and Gaillon owed to his drive.
britannica-1911-estrees-gabrielle-d:
Gabrielle d Estrees is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. She lived from 1573 to 1599 in France. She was the daughter of a marquis and his wife. King Henry the Fourth met her in late 1590. He fell deeply in love with her at that time. Her father wed her to a lord to keep her safe. That match proved unhappy and soon broke down.

From late 1592 she lived with the king as his close partner. She bore him more than one child. The king gave those children his name and rights. He trusted her and took her advice on affairs. He raised her rank step by step to duchess and peer. He hoped to wed her once his first union was annulled. She died in April 1599 before that could occur.
britannica-1911-etampes-anne-de-pisseleu:
Anne de Pisseleu d'Heilly, duchesse d'Etampes (1508 to about 1580), was the mistress of Francis I of France. She was the daughter of a Picardy noble, Guillaume de Pisseleu. She came to court before 1522 as a maid of honour to Louise of Savoy. The king made her his mistress, most likely on his return from captivity at Madrid in 1526. He soon set aside Madame de Chateaubriant for her.

Anne was lively, pretty, witty, and well read. She kept the king's favour to the end of his reign in 1547. The tie won some open honour: queen and mistress shared a window at a royal entry in 1530. In 1533 the king wed her to Jean de Brosse and made him duke of Etampes. Her sway at court grew large in the last years of the reign. She backed Admiral Chabot in court feuds.
britannica-1911-herbelot-de-molainville-:
Barthélemy d'Herbelot de Molainville (1625–1695) was a French orientalist, born in Paris on the 14th of December 1625. He studied at the university of Paris and took up Eastern languages. A year and a half in Italy improved them by talk with orientals at its ports, and there he met Holstenius and Leo Allatius. Back in France, Fouquet's household gave him a pension of 1,500 livres.

When Fouquet fell in 1661 the pension went, but Herbelot became secretary and interpreter of Eastern languages to the king. On a second Italian visit, Ferdinand II of Tuscany gave him many Eastern manuscripts and tried to keep him. Colbert recalled him, and the king restored his pension. In 1692 he took the chair of Syriac at the Collège de France. His Bibliothèque orientale filled nearly all his life. Finished in 1697 by A. Galland, it rests largely on Hadji Khalfa's great Arabic dictionary, much abridged.
britannica-1911-hervey-de-saint-denys-ma:
Marie Jean Léon Hervey de Saint Denys (1823–1892) was a French orientalist and man of letters, born in Paris. In 1851 he published a study of Chinese farming and gardening, on plants and animals fit to settle in the West. At the Paris Exhibition of 1867 he was commissioner for the Chinese exhibits.

In 1874 he followed Stanislas Julien in the chair of Chinese at the Collège de France. In 1878 he joined the Académie des Inscriptions et de Belles-Lettres. His books include T'ang poems rendered from the Chinese (1862) and an Ethnographie drawn from Ma-Touan-Lin (1876–1883). He also translated the Li-Sao (1870), wrote on Confucius (1887), and rendered Chinese tales valued for their light on Eastern custom. He died in Paris on the 2nd of November 1892.
britannica-1911-holbach-paul-heinrich-di:
Paul Heinrich Dietrich, Baron d'Holbach (1723–1789), was a French philosopher and man of letters of German origin, born at Heidelsheim in the palatinate in 1723. Rich and hospitable, he kept open house for the bold thinkers of the Encyclopédie circle: Diderot, D'Alembert, Buffon, Turgot, and guests such as Hume and Garrick.

For the Encyclopédie Holbach compiled and translated many articles on chemistry and mineralogy, from German. His own name rests on philosophy. Christianisme dévoilé (1767) attacked Christianity and religion as the source of all human evils. Le Système de la nature (1770), his most famous book, went further: it denied any deity and saw in the universe nothing but matter in movement. Souls, on this view, die with the body, and happiness is mankind's end. Religion's restraints were to give way to an education in enlightened self-interest.
britannica-1911-hondecoeter-melchior-d:
Melchior d'Hondecoeter (c. 1636–1695) was a Dutch painter, born at Utrecht about 1636 and dead at Amsterdam on the 3rd of April 1695. Old accounts make him grandson of Gillis and son of Gisbert d'Hondecoeter, and nephew of J. B. Weenix, who married into the family in 1638. Weenix plainly influenced his style. The relations of Gillis and Gisbert, both registered as painters at Utrecht in 1637, stay obscure.

The entry works through signed pictures to sort out the puzzle: a Concert of Birds of 1620 and a Hen and Chickens at Rotterdam both bear the monogram G. D. H., and landscapes with sportsmen raise the same question. Two artists seem to be in play, one painting birds and one landscapes. The bird painter is likely Gisbert, whose son Melchior chose birds as his own subject too. Weenix, as uncle, would naturally have taught his nephew the feathered tribe, the specialty that made Melchior's name.
britannica-1911-hozier-pierre-d:
Pierre d'Hozier, seigneur de la Garde (1592–1660), was a French genealogist, born at Marseilles on the 10th of July 1592. In 1616 he began wide researches into the pedigree of the kingdom's noble families. A prodigious memory for dates, names and kinships, joined to deep knowledge of heraldry, fitted him for the work. In 1634 he became historiographer and genealogist of France.

In 1641 d'Hozier was made juge d'armes of France, an office close to England's Garter king-of-arms. In 1643 he was set to verify the claims to nobility of the pages and equerries of the king's household. He gathered a great mass of documents but published little beside them. His chief works are the Recueil armorial des anciennes maisons de Bretagne (1638) and the names, arms and blazons of the knights of the order of the Saint-Esprit (1634). His papers became a quarry for later French genealogy.
clara-a-swain-m-d:
Clara A. Swain, M.D., by Mrs. Robert Hoskins, is a short biography of a medical missionary. Clara was the youngest of the ten children of John and Clarissa Seavey Swain. Born in Elmira, New York, she grew up in Castile, a frail and willful child whose mother taught her self-control early.

Her later work took her to India. At Bareilly she and her colleagues earned certificates from civil surgeons and an American physician, entitling them to practice in ordinary diseases. Need for a dispensary and hospital grew daily. It was met by the Nawab of Rampore, who gave an estate adjoining the mission premises for the purpose.
doe-osti-17027482-national-outlook-of-nu:
Three national laboratories joined in this August 31, 2026 outlook on nuclear power for data centers. Nicolas Stauff and So-Bin Cho of Argonne led authors from Idaho and Oak Ridge as well. Data center demand in the United States is projected to add roughly 12 to 84 gigawatts of average production need by 2030, the authors estimate.

Existing reactors, restarts, and power increases offer the most practical near term supply, though fleet size and licensing limit them. Announced deals could add about 6 gigawatts soon, with perhaps 50 gigawatts possible in the 2035 to 2040 window. Case studies and fuel cycle math follow, including uranium and enrichment needs if current reactors raise fuel enrichment slightly.
doe-osti-17038143-hierarchical-graph-bas:
Mina Priest and Trevor Steil of Lawrence Livermore built a clustering tool for huge data sets in project 24-ERD-024, reported in September 2026. Clustering groups similar points so analysts can spot regions of interest, outliers, and structure. Most scalable methods handled only low dimensional, plain coordinate data, a narrow slice of current billion point problems.

Their open source tool, ClaMS, adapts a density based method called HDBSCAN to graph data spread across many machines. Building the full distance graph for a billion points is impossible, so the team sampled sparse neighbor graphs and linked the pieces with new algorithms. A distributed routine then mines the cluster tree at full scale.
doe-osti-2583529-feasibility-assessment-:
Offshore wind in American waters faces a vessel problem, and report NREL/TP-5000-93817, dated December 20, 2024, studies a concrete way around it. Matthew Shields was NREL's contact under CRADA CRD-20-16570, working with RCAM. The idea joins two parts: a modular concrete suction pile support structure, and an installation approach that avoids scarce heavy lift vessels. Few Jones Act compliant lift ships exist, and conventional foundations carry environmental restrictions of their own.

Phase one produced a conceptual design sized for NREL's 15 megawatt reference turbine, structure, transport, and installation costs included. NREL estimated levelized cost of energy for a 1,005 megawatt plant across five permutations of support structure and installation method. The comparison tests whether concrete modules, built near shore and floated out, can undercut the steel-and-specialized-ship status quo. Feasibility, not final design, was the deliverable.
doe-osti-2587511-neutron-production-and-:
William Wampler of Sandia National Laboratories wrote this report, SAND2025-10823, printed in August 2025, on making and measuring neutrons at the Sandia Ion Beam Laboratory. Three nuclear reactions do the work: deuterium on deuterium, deuterium on carbon-12, and protons on lithium-7. Each turns an accelerator beam into a neutron source with known output.

Wampler works through the kinematics and cross sections of deuterium-deuterium neutron production on the laboratory's HVEE accelerator. Dosimetry then gets two treatments. Associated particle dosimetry counts the charged partner particle born with each neutron, while foil activation dosimetry infers the flux from the radioactivity induced in foils. One worked example reaches a steady reaction rate of 6.1 times ten to the eighth per second per microamp, with the activity decaying on a 14.4-minute characteristic time once the beam stops.
doe-osti-2588249-lightmat-seedling-proje:
Govindarajan Muralidharan of Oak Ridge National Laboratory wrote this final technical report, ORNL/LTR-2025/3997, for a LightMat seedling project on magnesium alloy sheet. Magnesium is the lightest structural metal in common use, and vehicles are the target. Cutting vehicle weight by 10 percent improves fuel economy by 6 to 8 percent in gasoline and diesel vehicles.

Swapping steel or aluminum parts for magnesium can save 25 to 75 percent of a part's weight. Candidate parts include decklid inners, seatback and roof panels, and door inners. Electric vehicles raise the stakes. A battery system two meters by 1.4 meters can weigh 700 kilograms, about a quarter of the whole vehicle. Its enclosure alone is roughly 20 percent of that weight and cost. The report develops high-strength magnesium sheet for such uses. It was rolled on Oak Ridge's mill, with rolls heated to 300 to 350 degrees Celsius and line speeds up to 500 feet per minute.
doe-osti-2588285-thermoreflectance-imagi:
James Loveless, Luke Yates, and Vincent Meyers of Sandia National Laboratories presented these slides, SAND2025-11081R, on thermoreflectance imaging of a Los Alamos MEMS device. Thermoreflectance turns tiny changes in surface reflectivity into temperature maps, letting engineers watch micro-devices heat in operation without touching them.

Calibration came first: on bare N-doped silicon, heating to 100 degrees Celsius gave a thermoreflectance coefficient averaging 1.5 times ten to the minus four, smaller than the published 3.4 times ten to the minus four for silicon at 470 nanometers. On device design number 3, the team measured the heating beams and the thermal actuator separately and together. The actuator alone reached 740 degrees at 6 volts. A surprise followed: significant heat appeared millimeters outside the device, 230 degrees with the actuator alone, even though the package thermally isolates it.
doe-osti-2589174-wec-sim-support-for-an-:
Thanh Toan Tran of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory is the technical contact for this CRADA final report, NREL/TP-5700-96578, dated September 2025, with Faete Filho sharing credit. The partner was East Carolina University, developing a wave-to-water desalination unit. A wave energy converter pressurizes seawater directly, in a supercritical system designed for zero discharge.

NREL's role was modeling support. The university needed foundational knowledge and proof of concept before scale-up and commercialization. NREL guided the use of its WEC-Sim based wave-to-water model, the open-source tool that simulates wave energy converters. The team also explored data exchange between WEC-Sim and ASPEN Plus, the process simulator handling the desalination chemistry side. Experimental data were used to validate the analytical models where possible. Wave motion sits on one side, high-pressure water treatment on the other. The two simulators must agree before anyone builds hardware.
doe-osti-2997311-arctic-impact-identific:
Diana Bull, Christopher Wentland, Kara Peterson, and Laura Swiler ask how little data can still reveal Arctic change, in Sandia report SAND2025-12027 dated September 2025. The Arctic warms faster than the rest of the planet, a pattern called polar amplification. Climate model archives are huge, and scanning all of them for every question is slow.

The exploratory project used the PAMIP model comparison data, which isolates the effect of sea ice loss. Winter season averages and daily distributions were compared across pre-industrial, present-day, and future runs. A statistical test at 95 percent confidence found the present-day distribution clearly distinct from pre-industrial only for Asian temperatures, a result the report presents as-is. Simpler forcing response models were then fit to see which variable relationships carry the signal, so later studies can sample less and learn more.
doe-osti-3000706-l-scie-and-supcrtne-mod:
Mavrik Zavarin, Eliott Chang, Luis Eguiguren and co-workers at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report database work in LLNL-TR-2010488, dated October 2025, for nuclear waste modelling. Predicting how radioactive elements creep through rock near a repository takes chemical thermodynamics: vast tables of how substances dissolve, bind and react. Two projects are covered, the L-SCIE sorption database and the SUPCRTNE thermodynamic model set, both needing data that agree with themselves.

One strand merges two internally consistent thermodynamic databases into one, with a workflow others can reuse. The other builds a community FAIR database of sorption, how radionuclides stick to mineral surfaces, to feed surface complexation and ion-exchange models. L-SCIE already holds nearly 73,000 data entries. A draft manuscript inside the report was condensed with help from the laboratory's own language model, then edited by the authors. The goal is livelier, more trustworthy reactive transport forecasts.
doe-osti-3007809-from-tides-to-seasons-h:
Carbon cycling where tides meet land is studied by Inke Forbrich of the Marine Biological Laboratory, with MBL and Oak Ridge National Laboratory team members, in the report for DOE award DE-SC0022108. The team built a new flux tower, AmeriFlux site US-PLo, on the Parker River in the Plum Island Ecosystems research area.

Wells, redox sensors, and novel optode probes tracked conditions in the marsh interior and creek bank, and the data tuned plant transport in the PFLOTRAN model. Measurements caught methane rising through the plants themselves: concentrations around green leaves built up at night and dropped at dawn as leaf pores opened. Tidal rhythm and plant physiology together set the marsh's carbon exchange.
doe-osti-3007910-conversion-of-anion-exc:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2025/3875, dated August 2025, works out how to convert used anion exchange resins to a citrate form fit for disposal. Its authors are Laetitia Delmau, Matt Warne, and Dennis Benker. Anion exchange resins are charged polymer beads used to separate and purify radioisotopes.

Close reading of the cited procedure showed its 'citrate' meant the dihydrogen citrate ion at pH 3.6, the form that actually pushes nitrate off the resin. Column tests on one-millilitre resin beds measured conversion step by step. A stronger 2 molar citrate solution turned syrupy and slowed the column, and sodium salicylate was tested as an alternative converting agent.
doe-osti-3010875-energy-efficient-large-:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Xinyi Shen, Bruno Jacob, Anne Chaka, and five co-authors, dated September 2025, attacks the energy cost of molecular dynamics simulation itself. The lever is numerical precision: most codes compute every number in double precision whether the physics needs it or not.

On a 64,000-atom liquid argon system at 100 kelvin, GPU packages and a single-precision Kokkos build were timed against the 64-CPU double-precision reference. Radial distribution functions from all versions overlapped completely, showing the cheaper arithmetic kept the physics. Mixed precision formats and hardware-aware code cut the computing bill for large simulations, where energy use is a real operating cost.
doe-osti-3010930-dynamics-of-electrified:
Electrified liquid surfaces under plasma contact are modelled in the final report for award DE-SC0023214, covering September 2022 to August 2025. Ken Hara led the work with Mikhail Shneider of the Princeton Collaborative Research Facility on plasma science and technology. The project studied how a plasma discharge deforms and drives a liquid surface it touches.

A shallow water model tracks the surface height as the interface evolves. Weighted least squares interpolation supplies the normal electric field on the moving surface, which couples the field solution back to the deformation. The report closes the award with the coupled model as its main product.
doe-osti-3013038-examining-the-impacts-o:
Susan van den Heever of Colorado State University led this project, award DE-SC0021160, running September 2020 to September 2025, with Mariko Oue of Stony Brook University and Stephen Saleeby. The question: how do feedbacks between cloud microphysics and air motion change deep convective clouds when the air carries different aerosol loads? The hosted record names no single report number; it is the project's final summary.

Using model intercomparison simulations of isolated storms over the Houston region, the team found a consistent warm-phase response in most cloud-resolving models. More aerosol suppressed warm rain, raised cloud water, and cut surface rainfall, with the strongest effects early in a storm's life. The ice-phase response, by contrast, flipped sign between models. The authors identify ice microphysics as a leading source of uncertainty in aerosol-storm research.
doe-osti-3029205-3d-mhd-simulations-for-: Shengtai Li of Los Alamos National Laboratory presented these slides on April 8, 2026, under the DOE INFUSE program. The thin deck's captioned frames cover three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations for an experiment setup called ECLAIR, proposed by Setthivoine You of Helicity Space. The setup changes both the initial and injection magnetic fields and adds a compressor field to squeeze the jet in the chamber. Frames report a peak core gun current of 82.2 kiloamps and a skin gun peak of 80.9 kiloamps. Other runs vary core gun current, including a zero-current case.
doe-osti-3030012-cummins-pem-fuel-cell-s:
Cummins reports final results under award DE-EE0009247 for a heavy-duty fuel cell system, in a project that ran from October 2020 to September 2025. Jean St-Pierre served as principal investigator, with Argonne National Laboratory, Dana, and W. L. Gore as partners. The goal was a modular polymer electrolyte membrane stack rated above 100 kilowatts. Stacks could then be combined to drive trucks and other heavy machines at up to 1 megawatt.
