One design push was heat: the stack must run at high pressure and shrug off peaks above 100 degrees Celsius. Integration work also flagged tight space for rejecting heat. Test chapters track hydrogen crossover through two Gore membrane types under stress protocols. One membrane build failed after 288 hours of harsh testing, with crossover up twenty-fold, while its sibling showed no such rise in the same span.
doe-osti-3030851-agent-based-bottom-up-m:
Thomas H. Bradley and Erika Gallegos of Colorado State University report final results on electric trucks in this research performance report. The project built agent-based, bottom-up models of medium- and heavy-duty electric vehicles. Agent-based means each truck and operator is simulated as its own decision maker, from the bottom up. The tools weigh purchase cost, running cost, daily duty, charging needs, and whether fleets will adopt the trucks at all.

One strand models charging-as-a-service, where a provider owns the chargers and sells fleets the power service instead. The report breaks that idea into economic, technical, and management functions. Another strand mines text with topic modeling to rank what buyers and operators talk about most, turning word patterns into saliency scores by category.
doe-osti-3362687-oes-co-sub-2-sub-pipeli:
Ayodeji Adeyemi, Younes Amjoun, and David Ammerman of Gulf Interstate Engineering wrote this design basis memorandum. It covers the OES carbon dioxide pipeline and was issued May 7, 2026. The work sits under the CarbonSAFE Phase III Illinois Storage Corridor project, led by Roland Okwen. The line will carry captured carbon dioxide from two ethanol plants near Gibson City, Illinois. It runs about 7.8 miles southeast to three injection wells outside Anchor, for permanent burial underground.

A design basis memorandum freezes the rules before detailed design: scope, codes, units, and material specs. Fitting tables here call out ASME flange and butt-weld standards by number. Bolts must meet ASTM A320 Grade L7. Heavy hex nuts must meet ASTM A194 Grade 7. Connections at 2 inches and up use raised faces. Fittings match the pipe wall and grade.
doe-osti-3365003-doe-early-career-projec:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38069 is the August 2025 annual report for Gavin Cornwell's DOE Early Career project on ice nucleating particles. Some airborne biological particles seed ice crystals in clouds, which changes how clouds reflect sunlight and produce precipitation. The project, running September 2024 to September 2025 in its first budget period, asks what controls how many of these particles ecosystems release.

First-year work centered on instruments and field preparation. Cornwell trained to run the WIBS and PINE particle instruments remotely at the ARM Bankhead National Forest site, and planned site visits and sample collection. A preliminary analysis decomposed ice nucleating particle spectra from other ARM sites with a statistical model that separates underlying particle types. The report is a progress account: capability built, campaigns ahead.
doe-osti-3365376-household-energy-use-in:
National Laboratory of the Rockies analysts Elaina Present, Eric Ringold, Florian Antretter, and seven co-authors profile household energy use across Pennsylvania's Delaware Valley. The housing stock analysis models single-family homes in the Philadelphia region, tying energy use, emissions, and utility bills to income, house characteristics, and end uses such as heating, cooling, and water heating. Energy affordability gets its own section.

A second half tests retrofit potential: packages of efficiency measures are applied to the modeled stock and the savings tallied. Results show where energy burdens fall hardest and which upgrades cut them most. Regional planners and program designers can see, for example, how bills vary by income band before choosing where to aim weatherization money. The report is a data portrait of one region's homes.
doe-osti-3365659-from-modular-adms-to-pl:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report PNNL-38909, by Andrew P. Reiman and Monish Mukherjee and dated May 2026, argues for rebuilding distribution grid operations software as a platform. Utilities run their local grids through Advanced Distribution Management Systems, traditionally one vendor's monolith. The report proposes a platform approach instead: a base system that hosts many swappable apps the way a phone hosts apps.

Modular design would let utilities add ambitious tools, from outage prediction to energy coordination, without replacing the whole system. The authors trace the path from today's modular products toward genuine plug-and-play operations, where applications install, update, and retire cleanly. For grid operators facing rooftop solar, electric vehicles, and batteries arriving faster than software buying cycles, that flexibility is the point.
doe-osti-3377606-tethered-balloon-system:
Atmospheric Radiation Measurement (ARM) report DOE/SC-ARM-26-025, dated July 2026, presents ozone profiles gathered by a tethered balloon system during the CoURAGE summer intensive period. The printed authors are P. Walter of St. Edward's University, J. Flynn and A. Ulinski of the University of Houston, and J. Sullivan of NASA Goddard Space Flight Center. The balloon site sat near the eastern shore of Chesapeake Bay.

The campaign, named CRGTBSO3, flew ozonesonde profiles to clarify how air composition differs inside and just above the marine layer. The balloon profiles are set beside NASA ozone lidars at the CoURAGE main site in Baltimore and at Hart Miller Island. Together they form an east-west line of vertical ozone profiles across the bay, though the report notes little overlap in data coverage between the instruments.
doe-osti-3377697-operating-experience-da:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-24-82553, also issued as NUREG/CR-7313 in June 2026, analyzes operating experience data for digital instrumentation and control systems in nuclear power plants. The authors are Tao Liu and Zhegang Ma. The subject is reliability and risk: how digital control systems actually fail in service, as plants replace older analog equipment.

The analysis works through confirmed digital control failures drawn from licensee event reports, separating hardware causes from software causes. Two failure modes dominate. In the first, parts such as processors, memory modules, or sensors stop working entirely, a complete loss of function. In the second, components keep running but produce output errors. The report uses that pattern to frame how risk assessment should treat digital systems differently from analog ones.
doe-osti-3740853-leveraging-gaussian-mix:
Sandia report SAND2026-25857, printed September 2026, offers a statistical way to flag odd readings in test data streams. Rudeger Wilke is the sole printed author. Fixed high and low limits miss slow drifts and odd shapes in a test data stream. Wilke instead fits a Gaussian mixture model to clean training runs. The fit carves the stream into zones of expected behaviour, one per phase of the signal.

New points are judged two ways. One test checks whether a point sits inside a window drawn along each zone's main axes. The other watches how a point bends the data's kurtosis, a measure of tail weight. Both tests update on the fly as fresh good data arrives. Worked examples use a synthetic current pulse with an in-rush spike and a settling tail. Open questions include which test suits which job.
doe-osti-3874836-a-frame-explicit-deriva:
Los Alamos report LA-UR-26-28271, issued September 15, 2026, rebuilds the motion equations for rigid bodies from first principles. Daniel Mills is the sole printed author, and the document is dated May 2026. Six-degree-of-freedom equations drive vehicle and spacecraft dynamics and control work. Mills targets bodies that change shape while keeping constant mass. The deeper complaint is notation: most books state frame facts in prose, leaving readers to track which frame each quantity lives in.

His notation encodes the object, its reference frame, and its resolving frame in every symbol. The derivation walks through centre of mass, translational momentum, and angular momentum in turn. Conservation laws close the system, and a calculus-of-variations route double-checks the result. Summarized equations collect the final forms in one place for direct use. The payoff is practical: fewer silent frame mix-ups in simulation code, because nothing about frames stays implicit.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBIDallasInvent: An FBI teletype sent on November 24, 1976 to the House Select Committee on Assassinations concerned inventories of records held in Dallas. The committee was then reopening the investigation of President Kennedy's death, and it needed to know what records existed. The surviving record gives the teletype's sender, recipient, date, and subject, but not the inventory itself.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FortDetrickBiol: Richard Lebherz wrote a piece titled Deterrent No. 7 about the biological warfare program at Fort Detrick, the Army's center for that work in Maryland. Germ warfare was a secret program discussed in public only in fragments. The surviving record gives the author, the title, and the subject but no date or contents, so the piece stands as a named article on the Detrick program.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-GlanzeWalterD_G: A letter filed under the name Walter D. Glanze explains the writer's attempt to secure a 60,000 dollar unsecured loan. The money was meant to pay off a debt to the Internal Revenue Service. The author's name cannot be recovered from the garbled text, so the letter survives as an unsigned account of one man's effort to borrow his way clear of the tax service.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JonesRonaldCoyD:
The Dallas County Medical Society issued a program for an evening at The Science Place on October 27, 1999. The guest was Dr. Ronald C. Jones. Jones had been Parkland Hospital's chief resident on November 22, 1963, and he relived his experience of the day President Kennedy was shot.

Doctors who worked on the dying president carried the day with them for life. Thirty-six years later, a hometown medical audience heard the chief resident tell it again. The program preserves the billing of that evening, when Dallas medicine remembered its most famous emergency in public.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MartinJohnJrDal:
FBI agents interviewed John Martin, Jr. on April 2, 1964, about a film he had made. Martin was superintendent of safety at the Dallas Post Office Terminal Annex. On November 22, 1963, he filmed the presidential motorcade with an 8mm movie camera. He then gave the film to Life magazine.

Amateur films of the motorcade became some of the most studied evidence in the case. Each one fixed the cars, the crowd, and the timing from a different spot. Martin's interview records who he was, where he stood, and what happened to his film afterward. It is the bureau's account of a witness whose evidence was pictures rather than words.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PatchenJerryD_P:
Harold Weisberg wrote to Jerry Patchen on December 15, 1974. He discusses the murder of Harvey St. Jean, a Miami lawyer. He also reports on his own affairs: the sales of his book, and his appearances on radio. Patchen was one of the correspondents with whom Weisberg shared case news.

The letter mixes the two registers of Weisberg's mail. First, a violent death in Miami that touched his network. Second, the business of being a self-published author: copies sold, broadcasts done. Letters like this kept his circle informed between book releases. They also show how much of his operation ran on personal correspondence, typed one letter at a time.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PepperWilliamFD:
Harold Weisberg wrote this memorandum on September 25, 1995, about a book by William Pepper. Pepper, a lawyer, had written on the King assassination. Weisberg says he distrusted Pepper for seeking access to his files without disclosing the book project. The memo also sets out Weisberg's criticism of the book itself.

Weisberg's files were his life's work, and he guarded them fiercely. A younger researcher asking for help while hiding a book struck him as a breach. The memo is written in his blunt late style, part grievance and part review. It records a falling-out between two men who agreed on much about the King case, and it shows how the movement's alliances broke on questions of credit.
govdocs-archive_org-tubes-4_Subterrene_N: A compilation called tubes-4 gathers material on subterrene machines, nuclear tunneling, and deep underground military bases. Its own file name adds the Illuminati and Freemasons to the mix. The library holds the set as an archive item, without backing, and classes it as fringe material. It serves readers who study underground-base lore, a durable branch of conspiracy writing about hidden places beneath the American desert.
grand-daddy-whiskers-m-d:
Nellie M. Leonard wrote Grand-Daddy Whiskers, M.D. as a tale of the woodfolk for young children, with pictures by Carle Michel Boog. The chapters open with a message from the woodfolk and a return to Pond Lily Lake. Then Grand-Daddy begins his work: he is the animals' doctor, and the tales show him setting a broken limb with deft paws.

Dot Squeaky holds a summer school; a woods fire calls out brave work, with Uncle Squeaky as captain. Wiggle borrows an automobile, twin tails cause trouble, and snow shuts the folk in for winter. Each chapter is a small adventure with a kind moral tucked inside. The animals talk, dress, and learn like children. It is a gentle storybook of the kind once read aloud at bedtime, full of lake, woods, and neighborly beasts.
holbach-letters-to-eugenia-microform-on-:
These letters to Eugenia were printed at London by R Carlile in 1819. The title page says they were first translated from the French of Fréret. It adds that they were supposed to be written by Baron Holbach. Their subject is the Christian religion's dogmas and mysteries, called absurd in the title itself.

Letter by letter, the writer presses a troubled lady's doubts. Prayer is mocked as an insult to a wise and just God. Priests, he argues, teach it to hold men's minds for their own gain. The tone is bold and scornful throughout. Readers meet the age's freethought at its most combative.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-d:
Part D is the fourth of six parts in the 1860 Virtue edition of David Hume's History of England. Hume wrote the history from 1754 to 1762, after his philosophy had met with cool reviews. The public took the history to its heart instead, and it stayed the standard account of England for generations.

From Caesar to 1688, Hume traces the slow growth of English law, liberty, and crown power. He writes as a judge above the fray, or tries to, and readers of every party quoted him. The edition holds the full seventy-one chapters across its six parts. Part D carries the story through its later, richer centuries.
illustrated-catalogue-of-a-portion-of-th:
William H. Holmes wrote this illustrated catalogue for the Bureau of Ethnology at the Smithsonian. It covers part of the finds made in the field season of 1881. The report was printed in Washington in 1884. Places named run from North Carolina and Tennessee toward the western mounds.

Each place gets lists of stone, clay, shell, and plant or animal goods. Cherokee finds, a mound on Pigeon River, and the McMahan Mound are among the entries. Later pages describe mounds in the west, with size and what digging found. The catalogue lets readers trace each object to its site.
incognita-or-love-and-duty-reconcil-d:
William Congreve wrote Incognita, a short prose romance of love and duty reconciled, before his fame as a dramatist of the Restoration stage. Congreve sets the tale in Florence, where two friends, Aurelian and Claudio, fall for ladies met at a tournament and a ball. Incognita is the name one heroine hides behind, and mistaken identity, disguise, and a near-duel keep the pairs apart.

Fathers, an unexpected marriage contract, and the claims of duty tangle the courtships before the reconciling of the title sorts them. Congreve tells it in balanced, witty prose that already shows the playwright's ear. The novella is brief enough for one sitting and polished enough to reward it, an early work by the author of The Way of the World.
memoirs-of-the-life-and-correspondence-o:
John Knox Laughton wrote the life and correspondence of Henry Reeve. Volume two of the two volume set stands here. Laughton taught modern history at King's College, London.

A portrait shows Reeve at sixty eight, from a photograph. Chapter thirteen treats the war in Italy, 1859 to 1860. Later heads treat law, letters, and church politics through the years. The Greville Memoirs, the Franco-German War, and his last years close the list. Outrage and disloyalty, French royalists, and retirement end the heads. A full life in law and letters fills the second volume.
mrs-mary-robinson-written-by-herself-wit:
